newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Rwandan refugees in Tanzania beaten, church torched.
newsitem.headline: Rwandan refugees in Tanzania beaten, church torched.

text.p: Suspected Tanzanian policemen burned down a church and beat Rwandan refugees sheltering inside to make them join the mass return of Hutus to Rwanda, aid officials said on Friday.

They said 28 Rwandan refugees staying at the church in the deserted Benaco refugee camp were attacked at night and forced to join a column of refugees trekking towards the Rusumo border crossing into Rwanda.
"Someone went in there and beat them. The church was burned down. No bodies were found," said a U.N. official in Ngara.
The aid officials, who declined to be identified, said suspicion for the attack rested on a Tanzanian police unit.

More than 250,000 Hutu refugees have gone back to Rwanda from Tanzania since a mass exodus began last Saturday. Tanzanian authorities have told all 540,000 Rwandan refugees to return their homeland by the end of December.
The refugees in the church had said they were waiting for God's word to return. A U.N. spokeswoman on Wednesday joked that the U.N. refugee agency hoped God would soon tell them to go.

Tanzanian security officials were not available for comment. Staff of the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) went to investigate the report. UNHCR officials said the incident may have happened on Wednesday night. Others said Thursday.

In another development, aid officials said they had found the bodies of three refugees apparently killed by machete blows. The body of a 15-year-old refugee was found near Lumasi camp and two other corpses were dumped near Benaco.
It was unclear who was responsible for the killings but in eastern Zaire last month Rwandan Hutu intimidators refusing to go to Rwanda killed refugees to force others to follow them.

Hutu hardliners, including former Rwandan troops and Interahamwe militiamen, refuse to return because they face being jailed or killed in Rwanda for their role in the genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates in 1994.
Overall, aid officials have praised the Tanzanian army for showing restraint during the repatriation operation.
"The army as far as we have seen have been very good," said a foreign aid worker on the road to Rwanda.

Aid officials however said Tanzanian security officers on Thursday had ordered Kitali camp closed and burned down all the schools there while Tanzanian troops ordered the nearby Keza camp closed and supervised the departure of some 5,000 people.
Hundreds of thousands of refugees, urged on by intimidators, fled the camps and headed deeper into Tanzania last week. But police and troops, at times wielding sticks, turned most around.

UNHCR has been criticised by the London-based human rights group Amnesty International for cooperating with the expulsion of refugees from Tanzania on the heels of more than 600,000 who streamed home from eastern Zaire last month.

UNHCR spokesman Paul Stromberg said 18,204 refugees crossed into Rwanda on Thursday, making a total of 254,000 to have returned since December 14 . The flow is slowing because groups trekking towards the border are spaced out.
UNHCR officials expected a 50-km (30-mile) column of more than 100,000 refugees to start arriving at the Rusumo crossing on Saturday. Many are exhausted after walking for six days.
Tanzanian troops are rounding up suspected intimidators and taking them to a special camp in the northwest. UNHCR has not been told how many are detained or what will happen to them.
Some 500 Rwandan refugees who fled from Tanzania to Uganda have been apprehended by Ugandan authorities, officials said.
